note.question: How can a planner allocate a scarce divisible resource and its associated cost or subsidy across income groups when households privately differ in resource utility and money is not quasilinear?
note.overview: The paper is a direct mechanism-design problem: households privately know resource utility and choose among income-dependent menus satisfying IC and IR.

models.summary: The paper is a direct mechanism-design problem: households privately know resource utility and choose among income-dependent menus satisfying IC and IR.
objects: Consumer households grouped by observable income and private resource-utility type

Resource-utility type g_j is private information
The planner knows the population shares theta_ij and utility functions/distributions
Consumer utility from the resource and money
decisions: Households report utility type indirectly by choosing a menu item
assumptions: There are finite ordered income groups and resource-utility types
Total utility is additively separable as G(s,g)+F(f+m), but money utility is concave and therefore nonquasilinear
G is concave and supermodular in resource and type; F is concave in final income
The planner must balance aggregate resource S and cost/subsidy M
Each offered bundle satisfies individual rationality and within-income-group incentive compatibility

models.method: The paper can then solve the problem of allocating the resource S first to maximize this objective, and then construct a monetary allocation that ensures the individual rationality and the incentive compatibility constraints.

sources.quote: The first-best solution ensures Pareto efficiency (no consumer can be strictly better off without making at least one of the consumers worse off) and individual rationality, but does not achieve incentive compatibil­ ity under our setting of allocating a divisible resource with non-quasi-linear utilities (Hurwicz 1972, Serizawa 2002).
